analysis.one_liner: Speeds up wildfire-prevention thinning near fire-prone communities, with grants to homeowners and tribes and limits on commercial logging.
analysis.headline: The bill got one Senate committee hearing in July 2003, was never voted out of committee, and died when that Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: After the severe wildfire seasons of the early 2000s, this bill would let the Forest Service and the Bureau of Land Management speed up thinning and prescribed burns around communities threatened by fire, skipping lengthy environmental reviews for smaller projects while requiring that most of the money go directly to those communities and drinking-water watersheds. It also sends $100 million a year to tribes, rural fire districts, and homeowner associations to clear brush around homes, bans commercial logging and log-skidding equipment in municipal watersheds, and forbids contractors from paying for work with trees. In exchange, it blocks administrative appeals and most lawsuits near at-risk communities, something the timber industry had been pushing for. The bill never came to a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: People living in or near fire-prone communities get faster treatment of the overgrown forests around their homes, with at least 70% of hazardous-fuels money required to be spent within a half mile of those communities or in municipal watersheds. Homeowner associations, local fire districts, tribes, and counties can get cost-share grants to clear brush around houses and restore burned ground. Small timber businesses in poor rural communities get a guaranteed share of contracts, and Forest Service employees keep protection from being replaced by private contractors.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Fire-prone communities, tribes, and rural small businesses

how_it_helps.text: It lets agencies speed up hazardous fuels reduction — thinning, brush removal, and prescribed fire — around communities at risk of wildfire, without preparing an environmental assessment or impact statement, for projects that stay under a cap of 250,000 board feet of merchantable wood (or 1 million board feet of salvage).

It requires agencies to spend at least 70% of annual hazardous fuels funds inside a half mile of at-risk communities or in municipal watersheds, directing the money to where people and drinking water are actually threatened rather than to remote backcountry projects.

It requires at least 30% of those funds to go to projects benefiting small businesses that use small-diameter wood, located in small economically disadvantaged communities, and mandates local-preference contracting so byproducts are processed locally.

It provides $100 million a year for fiscal 2004-2008 to reduce wildfire risk to structures and restore burned areas on tribal lands, nonindustrial private lands, and state lands, including cost-share grants to Indian tribes, local fire districts, municipalities, homeowner associations, and counties to clear hazardous fuels around homes.

It protects drinking water and old forests: no timber sales or log skidding machines in municipal watersheds absent extraordinary circumstances, no new roads in inventoried roadless areas, and a requirement to maintain mature and old-growth stands while 'thinning from below.'

It bans goods-for-service contracting (giving trees to contractors in exchange for work), requires all project revenues to go to the Treasury rather than subsidize logging, and establishes a monitoring commission with equal representation from conservation, community, and commodity interests plus public access to monitoring data.

It exempts the Forest Service from the Competitive Sourcing Initiative (OMB Circular A-76), the administration program that would have forced public firefighting and land-management jobs to compete against private contractors, and adds $250 million in borrowing authority so suppression funding does not run dry mid-fire.

The expedited process expires after five years, applies projects through a collaborative local process with tribes, agencies, and landowners at the table, and excludes wilderness study areas and lands where logging is restricted by law.

analysis.who_pays: If passed, the bill costs the Treasury about $125 million a year in mandatory spending ($25 million for insect research, $100 million for wildfire risk reduction and burned-area restoration) without a separate appropriation. Large timber contractors lose goods-for-service deals and face project-level caps on merchantable wood, and the timber industry as a whole gets less access than broader expedited-logging proposals offered. Conservation groups lose the appeals and lawsuits they use to slow or shape projects in community protection zones.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large timber contractors and the Treasury

drawbacks.text: For projects in community protection zones and municipal watersheds, the agency's decision to skip environmental review is 'conclusive as a matter of law' and cannot be challenged in court, so even a poorly sited or poorly designed treatment near homes would face no independent check.

The bill commits mandatory money without a separate appropriation: $25 million a year for insect research and $100 million a year for wildfire risk reduction and burned-area restoration, drawn directly from Treasury during fiscal 2004 through 2008.

It opens up to 20 million additional acres to expedited treatment on top of the roughly 2.5 million acres already treated each year, a scale-up that could outpace monitoring and follow-up maintenance.

Supporters of faster treatment would object that the bill's constraints — a cap of 250,000 board feet of merchantable wood per project, a ban on log skidding in municipal watersheds, and a prohibition on trading trees to contractors for work — could slow projects enough to blunt the safety gains the expedited process was meant to deliver.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are concrete and aimed where the danger is: money and treatments focused on the half-mile around fire-prone communities, grants to homeowners and fire districts, dedicated funding for tribal lands, and a five-year sunset with monitoring to check whether it worked. The costs are real but constrained: it skips environmental review and blocks lawsuits for a defined class of projects near communities and watersheds, which removes a check even when a project is badly designed, and it commits $125 million a year without an annual vote. An honest supporter would acknowledge the bill traded away meaningful environmental process to win speed, though far less of it than the broader logging bill that became law instead; an honest critic of expedited treatment would have to concede the bill barred commercial logging and heavy equipment in the very watersheds it expedites and capped the wood that could be removed.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate's energy committee held one hearing on the bill, then nothing: no vote in committee, no floor vote, and the bill expired when that Congress ended in January 2005.

narrative.text: Senator Bingaman introduced the bill on June 23, 2003 with three Democratic cosponsors: Tom Daschle, Patty Murray, and Maria Cantwell.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources the same day.
The committee held a hearing on July 22, 2003 (printed as S.Hrg. 108-140), but the bill was never reported out, and no further action was taken before the Congress ended on January 3, 2005.

The bill was written as a compromise: it included the expedited categorical-exclusion process that the timber industry and the administration wanted, but paired it with a community-funding mandate, logging limits, a ban on appeals and lawsuits only within narrowly defined zones, a five-year sunset, and mandatory monitoring.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The competing, less-restrained approach moved ahead instead: the Bush administration and congressional Republicans had already pushed their own forest bill with broader expedited-logging authority, which was signed into law in December 2003 as the Healthy Forests Restoration Act. That law gave the timber industry faster project approvals with weaker environmental review than Bingaman's bill would have allowed, while fire-prone communities got fewer of the targeted funding guarantees this bill contained.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Timber operators and the competing expedited-logging law

for.name: Jeff Bingaman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and sponsored it through the Energy and Natural Resources Committee, which held a hearing on it.

for.name: Tom Daschle
for.role: Senate Minority Leader, U.S. Senator from South Dakota

against.name: Pete Domenici
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources
against.what_they_did: His committee held one hearing on the bill in July 2003 but never scheduled a markup or reported it to the floor, and the bill died there.

against.name: President George W. Bush
against.what_they_did: Pushed a competing forest bill with broader expedited-logging provisions and weaker environmental review, which Congress passed and he signed into law in December 2003, replacing the debate this bill had entered.

sides.party_line_note: All five senators behind the bill were Democrats, and the competing forest bill that became law that December was advanced by a Republican president and a Republican Senate majority; no roll-call vote was ever taken on this bill.

industries.note: The bill gives timber operators faster fuels-reduction projects with no administrative appeals and no court review near communities, which the industry wanted. But it caps merchantable wood per project, bars log skidding in municipal watersheds, forbids goods-for-service deals, and sends all project revenue to the Treasury, so the commercial upside is deliberately limited.

industries.industry: Small-diameter wood products businesses in disadvantaged communities
industries.note: At least 30% of hazardous fuels funds must benefit small businesses that process small-diameter material and woody debris, and contracting must use local preference. This directs public money toward rural small businesses rather than large contractors.

industries.industry: Federal Forest Service and land-management workforce
industries.note: The bill exempts the Forest Service from the Competitive Sourcing Initiative, the program that would have put federal land-management jobs up for bid against private contractors. Employees keep their jobs, and the public keeps an in-house firefighting force.

Conservation groups lose the administrative appeals and court challenges they use to shape or stop fuels projects near communities, and get only a monitoring commission and a seat in the collaborative process in exchange. The bill's conclusive-presumption provision is the sharpest loss, though it is narrower than the broader review exemptions in the law that eventually passed.
